title: Initial Access via CVE-2024-35250 Kernel Streaming Exploitation

status: experimental
description: Detects the initial access phase of CVE-2024-35250 exploitation where a local user-mode process sends a crafted IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY request to MSKSSRV kernel driver with KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET flag, indicating an attempt to trigger privilege escalation through a double-fetch vulnerability.
references:

    - https://devco.re/blog/2024/08/23/streaming-vulnerabilities-from-windows-kernel-proxying-to-kernel-part1-en/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-03
tags:
    - attack.privilege-escalation
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.t1068
    - attack.t1211
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY'
            - 'KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET'
            - 'KSPROPSETID_DrmAudioStream'
            - 'KsSynchronousIoControlDevice'
            - 'RequestorMode.*KernelMode'
        Image|endswith: '\mskssrv.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative tools using kernel streaming APIs
    - Development environments with kernel debugging utilities
level: high

attack_vector.reasoning: The write-up clearly describes a local privilege escalation exploit using kernel streaming drivers with specific IOCTL patterns and memory handling issues. The attack starts from a local user-mode process interacting with kernel drivers, making the local protocol and preconditions clear. pipeline.attack_summary: Threat actors exploit CVE-2024-35250 in the Microsoft Kernel Streaming Service (MSKSSRV) to perform local privilege escalation by manipulating IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY requests with KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET flag, allowing arbitrary kernel function calls through a double-fetch vulnerability. The attack leverages a proxy-based logical flaw in kernel I/O handling where RequestorMode is incorrectly set during nested IOCTL calls, bypassing security checks and enabling elevation of privilege from user to system level.

Taiwanese cybersecurity company DEVCORE, which discovered and reported CVE-2024-35250, shared additional technical details in August 2024, stating it's rooted in the Microsoft Kernel Streaming Service (MSKSSRV)

The function where IoBuildDeviceIoControlRequest is used in Kernel Streaming is in ks!KsSynchronousIoControlDevice and it obviously involves calling IOCTL in the kernel using the aforementioned method. However, it appears that Irp->RequestorMode is properly set here, and different values are assigned based on the parameters of KsSynchronousIoControlDevice. This will be a convenient library for kernel streaming driver developers

ks.sys is one of the core components of Kernel Streaming. It is the library of Kernel Streaming responsible for forwarding requests such as IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY to the corresponding device driver, and it also handles functions related to AVStream
The most important ones are ksthunk.sys and ks.sys. Almost all functionalities are related to them. portcls.sys is mostly used for PCI and DMA-based audio device hardware drivers
We can set these properties through IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY

If we give the property set as KSPROPSETID_DrmAudioStream, there is additional processing at [5]. At [6], we can see that it first checks whether Irp->RequestorMode is KernelMode(0). If it is called from user, it will directly return an error

In the IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY of Kernel Streaming, to increase efficiency, KSPROPERTY_TYPE_SERIALIZESET and KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET requests are provided to allow users to operate on multiple properties through a single call
When we initially send IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY, we use the existing property KSPROPSETID_Service of MSKSSRV for subsequent operations

This vulnerability was discovered shortly after CVE-2023-29360 was released. It was already being exploited when Microsoft released their patches. This is a very easily discovered vulnerability. It uses the objects (FSContextReg, FSStreamReg) stored in FILE_OBJECT->FsContext2 for subsequent processing. However, there is no check on the type of FsContext2, leading to type confusion

The first one is the vulnerability used by Synacktiv in Pwn2Own Vancouver 2023. This is a logical vulnerability in the MSKSSRV driver. When MSKSSRV uses MmProbeAndLockPages to lock user-specified memory address as framebuffer, the AccessMode was not set correctly. This leads to a failure to check whether the user-specified address belongs to the user space. If the user provides a kernel address, it will map the specified kernel address to user space for the user to use. Ultimately, this allows the user to write data to any address in the kernel

attack_vector.reasoning: The write-up clearly describes how attackers compromise routers and use Winbox Loader to download malicious DLLs, which is the primary method of initial access. The text emphasizes this as a unique infection vector and provides sufficient detail about the attack surface.

pipeline.attack_summary: The Slingshot APT uses a complex multi-stage attack involving compromised Mikrotik routers to deliver malicious DLLs via Winbox Loader. The infection begins with downloading a modified ipv4.dll from the router's file system, which then downloads additional components. It leverages vulnerable drivers for kernel-mode execution and employs sophisticated modules like Cahnadr/NDriver and GollumApp for persistence, data collection, and exfiltration.

indicators.context: The name appears unencrypted in some of the malicious samples – it is the name of one of the threat actor’s components, so we decided to extend it to the APT as a whole.
The initial loader replaces the victim's legitimate Windows library 'scesrv.dll' with a malicious one of exactly the same size.
One of them – ipv4.dll – has been placed by the APT with what is, in fact, a downloader for other malicious components.

When the target user runs Winbox Loader software (a utility used for Mikrotik router configuration), this connects to the router and downloads some DLLs (dynamic link libraries) from the router’s file system.
Following infection, Slingshot would load a number of modules onto the victim device, including two huge and powerful ones: Cahnadr, the kernel mode module, and GollumApp, a user mode module.
Canhadr, also known as NDriver, contains low-level routines for network, IO operations and so on.

The most sophisticated module is GollumApp. This contains nearly 1,500 user-code functions and provides most of the above described routines for persistence, file system control and C&C communications.
During our research we also found a component called KPWS that turned out to be another downloader for Slingshot components.
These vulnerabilities include CVE-2007-5633; CVE-2010-1592, CVE-2009-0824.
These vulnerabilities include CVE-2007-5633; CVE-2010-1592, CVE-2009-0824.

We were able to find several cases where the attackers got access to Mikrotik routers and placed a component downloaded by Winbox Loader, a management suite for Mikrotik routers.
I know the Technicolor TC8717T Wireless Telephony DOCSIS 3.0 Modem, 4 Port Router which comes with ISP Xfinity, has been harnessed this attack.
The ISP Xfinity (Comcast) would eventually confirm that my network had been compromised

attack_vector.reasoning: The text clearly describes a phishing email with a hyperlink leading to a download link for the malware. The initial access is social engineering via email, and subsequent behavior is well-documented in terms of execution and persistence mechanisms.

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack begins with a phishing email containing a hyperlink to a malicious 7z file hosted on MediaFire. When the user clicks the link, the file is downloaded and extracted to reveal a NetWire RAT executable. The malware uses anti-analysis techniques like dynamic code extraction and anti-sandboxing to evade detection. It then establishes persistence via registry keys, collects system information, and communicates with a C2 server (gbam0001.duckdns.org) to send data. The infection chain also involves GuLoader as an initial dropper that retrieves NetWire from encrypted files hosted on various domains.

indicators.context: The downloaded file is a 7z file, which contains the new variant of NetWire RAT.
After decompressing it, we are able to get an EXE file with the name of "PROFORMA-INVOICE 0990.exe".
The malware file download link is: "hxxps[:]//www[.]mediafire[.]com/file/d86hz5qj21lmhrb/PROFORMA-INVOICE_0990.7z/file".
Its domain is found in the decrypted string, which for this variant is "gbam0001.duckdns[.]org:3366".
NetWire continues to create its home key (HKCU\SOFTWARE\NetWire) as well as adding it into the auto-run group in the victim's registry.
It checks to see if the current executable file is located in the correct folder (%AppData%\Install) and has the right file name (Host.exe).
NetWire creates a log folder to store the log files of information that it collects from the victim's system. The log folder is located at "%AppData%\Logs".
If not, it relocates the file into "%AppData%\Install" and renames it as "Host.exe".
It calls the API USER32.GetCursorPos() twice to obtain two mouse cursor positions and then compares them.
It also calls the API ntdll.ZwGetContextThread to obtain the current thread context structure, which contains the CPU debug register status.
call dword ptr [ebp+110]     ;kernel32.GetCurrentThread
mov eax, dword ptr [edi+4000]  ;Key API address, like kernel32.CreateProcessInternalW
Next, it initializes several global variables and Windows Sockets by calling the API WSAStartup().
Once NetWire receives the "9B" command, Task_Fun() handles it in a sub procedure which collects the victim's computer basic information and sends it back to the C&C server.
Current login User name collected by calling the API GetUserNameA() or from the system environment variable.
Victim's Computer name by calling the API GetComputerNameA().
Victim's Windows version information by calling the API GetVersionExA().
1. Obtains a time value how long the victim has been inactive since the last input. Command number: 097h
2. Executes a downloaded executable file or an existing local file like "cmd.exe". Command numbers: 09Ch, 09Ch, 0A3h, 0AFh, 0B6h, 0C3h

3. Performs actions including: exit NetWire process, close the socket to C&C server, read a value from its home key in the system registry, reset or delete a specified registry key, delete the NetWire executable file and relocate its executable file ("Host.exe"). Command numbers: 09Fh, 0A0h, 0A1h, 0A2h, 0AEh, 0E5h, 0E7h

5. Steals and collects credentials stored in the victim's system by different software. It focuses on these: 360Chrome, Opera, Mozilla Firefox, Mozilla SeaMonkey, Google Chrome, Comodo Dragon browser, YandexBrowser, Brave-Browser, Mozilla Thunderbird, Microsoft Outlook and Pidgin. It also reads the victim's browser history records from the history folder. Command numbers: 0D4h, 0D5h, 0D6h, 0D7h, 0D8h, 0D9h.

7. Obtains window handles that are created on the victim's device; sends a windows message to a window by specified windows handle; obtains information of all running processes on the victim's device; kills a running process using a given process ID; obtains a list of TCP or UDP endpoint information (TCP or UDP, local and remote IP address, port, status) as well as the process information (process name, process id) that connects this endpoint. Command numbers: 0BEh, 0C0h, 0C1h, 0C2h, 0E3h.

8. Collects the victim's computer basic information, which include the current username, logon session information, computer name, CPU information, Windows version, memory status, network status, and Windows installation path. It also collects the PowerShell installation path, NetWire executable file full path, and its Log folder full path, etc. Command numbers: 0BAh, 0BCh.

9. Controls the victim's input devices, including the Keyboard and Mouse. By sending keybd_event and mouse_event, it can simulate Keyboard and Mouse operations. Command numbers: 0C5h, 0C6h, 0C7h, 0C8h.
GuLoader is a file downloader that was first discovered in December 2019, and it has been used to distribute a wide variety of remote administration tool (RAT) malware.
NetWire is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) malware that has been widely used for many years.

status: experimental
description: Detects the execution of Microsoft Office processes (e.g., winword.exe, excel.exe) that load macro-enabled Office documents (.docm, .xlsm), which is a common initial access vector used in phishing campaigns.
references:

date: 2026-10-03

    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.t1204
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\msaccess.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '.docm'
            - '.xlsm'
            - '.pptm'
            - '.dotm'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate use of macro-enabled Office documents in trusted environments
level: high

attack_vector.reasoning: The write-up clearly describes exploitation of a vulnerability in Veeam Backup & Replication through an unauthenticated network request on port 9401, followed by SQL shell command execution that triggers PowerShell script download and execution. The attack chain is well-defined with clear telemetry indicators.

pipeline.attack_summary: FIN7 or a threat actor utilizing FIN7 tradecraft targeted Veeam Backup & Replication servers via unauthenticated access through CVE-2023-27532 (port 9401), executing PowerShell scripts including POWERTRASH for initial compromise. They used SQL shell commands to trigger execution, performed reconnaissance with netstat, tasklist, ipconfig, and WMI queries, stole credentials using a PowerShell script, established persistence via DUBLOADER (a custom loader mimicking libcurl.dll) that drops multiple files including an encoded DICELOADER payload, and conducted lateral movement using WMI and SMB. The attack chain included initial access, execution, persistence, lateral movement, credential access, and discovery.

indicators.context: An SQL server process related to the Veeam Backup instance executed a shell command
Obfuscated loader written in PowerShell that has been attributed to FIN7
An additional file called "445.ps1" was dropped and executed on the compromised Veeam backup servers
PowerShell script filenames used for these PowerShell scripts were identical to the naming convention reportedly used by FIN7
PowerShell script filenames used for these PowerShell scripts were identical to the naming convention reportedly used by FIN7
A custom PowerShell script, "gup18.ps1", was executed to set up an active foothold in the compromised machine

This unique PowerShell script has not been previously seen in the attack arsenal of FIN7, and we are now tracking it as POWERHOLD. The script was hosted on an external file-hosting service "temp[.]sh"

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include gup.exe – Legitimate GUP.exe binary (part of the Notepad++ application)

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include gup.xml – Configuration file that's part of the GUP application

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include libcurl.dll – .NET DLL file side-loaded by gup.exe

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include JZ4qWKZW – Encoded DICELOADER payload that's loaded and executed by libcurl.dll

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include jkBDfXaL.bat – Batch file that executes gup.exe

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files include 0JNvHvAz.vbs – VBScript file that executes the batch file

The crafted loader is designed to mimic the legitimate libcurl.dll file by including export function names found in the legitimate version and thus imported by the GUP executable. Only one of the export functions, namely "curl_easy_init" contains malicious code. This unique loader has not been previously seen in FIN7's attack arsenal, and we are now tracking it as DUBLOADER
The affected servers had TCP open port 9401 exposed to the internet. This port is used for communication with the Veeam Backup Service over SSL

To resolve the list of collected IP addresses to their respective host names, a custom PowerShell script, "host_ip.ps1", was executed. The PowerShell script content is nearly identical to a code snippet shared online for resolving IP to Hostname with PowerShell

The threat actor launched a custom PowerShell script (explained above) to gather information about the target host. This was followed by the execution of another PowerShell script, which was another POWERTRASH sample. This script performed remote injection into the 'PlugPlay' service

The threat actor used a series of commands as well as custom scripts to gather host and network information from the compromised machines. Some of these commands included: netstat  : Display all active TCP connections and listening ports

pipeline.attack_summary: Raspberry Robin is a multi-stage worm that initially spreads via infected USB drives containing LNK files disguised as folders. Upon insertion, it executes cmd.exe to launch msiexec.exe which installs malicious payloads from compromised QNAP NAS devices. The malware uses living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) such as rundll32.exe, odbcconf.exe, and control.exe for execution, and persists via the RunOnce registry key. It has evolved to deploy other malware families like FakeUpdates, IcedID, Bumblebee, and TrueBot, often leading to hands-on-keyboard attacks by groups such as DEV-0243 (EvilCorp) and DEV-0950 (FIN11/TA505), ultimately facilitating ransomware deployment including LockBit, Clop, and others.

pipeline.attack_summary: An attacker exploited CVE-2023-27532 to gain unauthenticated access to Veeam Backup & Replication servers via TCP port 9401, executing PowerShell scripts (POWERTRASH) for initial compromise. The attack chain includes in-memory execution, credential theft, discovery commands, lateral movement using WMI and SMB, and persistence via a custom loader (DUBLOADER) that uses a malicious libcurl.dll to execute DICELOADER on startup.

references:
    - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-26084
    - https://confluence.atlassian.com/doc/confluence-security-advisory-2021-08-25-1077906215.html
    - https://github.com/h3v0x/CVE-2021-26084_Confluence
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/006/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-03
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.t1190
    - attack.t1213.001
    - attack.t1588.006
    - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection1:
        cs-uri-query|regex: '\$\{.*\}'
    selection2:
        cs-uri-query|contains: 'queryString='
    selection3:
        cs-uri-query|contains: 'createpage-entervariables.action'
    condition: 1 of selection*
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using similar patterns in query strings
    - Internal tools or monitoring agents that may use OGNL-like syntax in non-malicious contexts
level: high

description: Identifies potential execution of malicious code through OGNL injection in Confluence Server/Data Center by detecting specific OGNL expression syntax in HTTP requests.
references:

author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-03
tags:

logsource:

detection:

        cs-uri-query|regex: '\[\['

The advisory and PoC both emphasize the exploitation via HTTP requests to specific endpoints with attacker-controlled parameters, making the attack vector highly observable and well-defined.

pipeline.attack_summary: An unauthenticated attacker exploits CVE-2021-26084 in Atlassian Confluence Server and Data Center to perform OGNL injection, enabling arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability affects specific versions before 6.13.23, from 6.14.0 before 7.4.11, from 7.5.0 before 7.11.6, and from 7.12.0 before 7.12.5. Attackers can leverage this to gain control over affected systems.
